How Unrecognized Trade Secrets and Intangible Assets Impact Corporate Balance Sheets

The Hidden Scale of Corporate Intangible Assets

Corporate intangible assets reached nearly $97 trillion globally in 2025, marking a 23% increase from the prior year, according to data from the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO). Despite this massive global valuation, standard corporate accounting practices keep an estimated 79% to 83% of intangible asset value hidden off corporate balance sheets.

Mary Guzman, Founder and CEO of Crown Jewel Insurance, recently discussed these figures and the underlying mechanics of intellectual property protection on the Disruption Interruption Podcast hosted by Karla Jo Helms. Guzman noted that while much attention traditionally centers on formal patents, a vast portion of corporate value resides in trade secrets—the confidential processes, internal know-how, strategies, and operational data that provide companies with a competitive advantage without public disclosure.

Valuation Challenges and the Limits of Cyber Insurance

As businesses rely more heavily on proprietary software workflows, supply-chain logistics, and consumer data, the risks surrounding unauthorized disclosures or departing employees grow. Guzman pointed out that while cyber insurance markets have evolved to cover ransomware, privacy liabilities, and business interruption, the financial value of core research and development (R&D) and intellectual property has largely remained excluded from traditional policies.

A central hurdle for insurers has been the difficulty of evaluating proprietary know-how before a legal dispute or court ruling establishes its status as a protected trade secret. When an employee leaves with sensitive company information, impacted firms often struggle to quickly prove what the trade secret was, whether reasonable protective measures were maintained, and if insiders understood the information's confidentiality. According to Guzman, many organizations discover gaps in their documentation only after a potential theft occurs, leading to costly and time-consuming retrospective discovery.

Proactive Valuation and Financing Implications

Crown Jewel Insurance focuses on identifying and assessing proprietary information before disputes arise. This process involves calculating development costs, including unsuccessful iterations and "negative know-how" that might prevent competitors from repeating the same R&D errors. Documenting these protective measures aims to provide legal counsel with concrete evidence should an injunction become necessary, while insurance coverage helps address related legal and forensic expenses.

Guzman also highlighted potential implications for founders, chief financial officers, lenders, and investors. Assigning a defensible value to off-balance-sheet trade secrets can influence asset protection, enterprise value, and financing discussions, offering residual value that could be licensed or sold if a venture faces financial distress.

Practical Implications and Verification

Readers evaluating trade secret management and intangible asset valuation should consider several confirmed details alongside existing industry uncertainties:

  • What is Confirmed: According to WIPO data, global intangible assets reached approximately $97 trillion in 2025, with standard accounting rules leaving 79% to 83% of that value off corporate balance sheets. Trade secrets encompass non-public processes, internal strategies, and operational know-how.
  • What Remains Unclear: The degree to which insurers will broadly adopt specialized underwriting for trade secret values before formal legal disputes, and how uniformly courts will assess pre-loss valuations during litigation, remain subject to market evolution.
  • How to Verify: Readers can review the original discussion and context via the [Disruption Interruption Podcast](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/disrupting-intellectual-property-mary-guzman-insures-the-how-behind-innovation-302923942.html) or consult global intangible asset metrics directly through the World Intellectual Property Organization.
